f.why: ADD waits 2 cycles for LDUR's WB. SUB then sits right before ORR, so ORR waits 2 more for SUB's WB: 4 stalls, 12 cycles in all.

f.q: Full forwarding again, but the first line is ADDI X10, X20, #0 instead of the load. How many stall cycles?
f.why: Every value now comes from the ALU, and forwarding delivers each one in time: 0 stalls.

f.q: Full forwarding, but the third line is LDUR X13, [X20, #8] instead of the SUB. How many stall cycles?
f.why: Now there are two load-use pairs (LDUR → ADD and LDUR → ORR), one bubble each: 2 stalls.

questions.q: A program sums the brightness of every pixel in a large image. Each pixel is 4 bytes, and the program reads every pixel exactly once, in order of increasing address. The data cache uses 64-byte blocks, and most of these reads hit. Why?
o: Each pixel is read again soon after, so it is still in the cache (temporal locality)
One miss also loads the next pixels, so the reads after it hit (spatial locality)
Changed pixels reach main memory only when their block is evicted (write-back)
The loop works on small tiles that are each reused many times over (blocking)
questions.kid: You need the next 16 pages of a book, one after another. Instead of walking to the shelf for each page, you carry the whole chapter to your desk on the first trip, so the next 15 pages are already there. Using things that sit next to what you just used is spatial locality.
questions.why: Spatial locality means addresses near a recent access are likely to be used soon. Each miss loads a 64-byte block holding 64 ÷ 4 = 16 pixels, so one miss is followed by 15 hits, a 15/16 ≈ 94% hit rate. Temporal locality does not help here, because no pixel is read twice.
w: Each pixel is read exactly once, so no address is reused soon; temporal locality is not what produces these hits.
The loop only reads pixels, and write-back only changes when stores reach memory; it cannot turn a first read into a hit.
The loop makes one straight pass with no tiles and no reuse; blocking is a different technique for code that revisits data.

f.q: A paint program re-reads the same pixel under the brush thousands of times in a row. Why do those reads keep hitting?
f.why: The same address is used again and again within a short time. That is temporal locality: after the first miss, the pixel stays in the cache and every later read hits.

f.q: A program stores to the same pixel 1,000 times in a row, yet main memory receives a single write for it, when its block finally leaves the cache. Which policy explains this?
f.why: A write-back cache updates the block in place and marks it dirty. Memory is written once, when the dirty block is evicted. A write-through cache would send all 1,000 stores toward memory.

questions.q: A 2-way set-associative data cache holds 32 KiB of data in 64-byte blocks. Physical addresses are 40 bits, and memory is byte addressed. How many bits of each address go to the tag, the set index and the block offset?
o: Tag 25, index 9, offset 6
Tag 29, index 8, offset 3
Tag 27, index 7, offset 6
Tag 26, index 8, offset 6
questions.kid: Read an address like a mailing label. The last 6 bits are the apartment number: which of the 64 bytes in the block you want. The next 8 bits are the street: which of the 256 sets to search. The rest is the family name (the tag) you check on the mailbox to be sure the block there is yours.
questions.why: Blocks = 32 KiB ÷ 64 B = 512. Sets = 512 ÷ 2 ways = 256, so index = log<sub>2</sub> 256 = 8 bits. Offset = log<sub>2</sub> 64 = 6 bits, because every byte must be addressable. Tag = 40 − 8 − 6 = 26 bits.
w: Index 9 means 512 sets, which is the direct-mapped count; with 2 ways the 512 blocks form only 256 sets.
The offset must pick one byte of 64, which takes 6 bits; 3 bits would only pick one of 8 doublewords.
Index 7 means 128 sets, which is what a 4-way cache would have; 2 ways give 256 sets and 8 index bits.

f.q: Same 32 KiB cache with 64-byte blocks and 40-bit addresses, but now direct-mapped. How do the address bits split?
f.why: Direct-mapped means one block per set, so 512 sets need 9 index bits. The offset is still 6 bits, leaving a tag of 40 − 9 − 6 = 25 bits.

f.q: Same 32 KiB cache with 64-byte blocks and 40-bit addresses, but now 4-way set associative. How do the address bits split?
f.why: 512 blocks ÷ 4 ways = 128 sets, so the index is 7 bits. The offset stays 6 bits, and the tag is 40 − 7 − 6 = 27 bits.

f.q: A smaller 2-way cache holds 4 KiB in 8-byte blocks, still with 40-bit byte addresses. How do the address bits split?
f.why: 4 KiB ÷ 8 B = 512 blocks, and 512 ÷ 2 ways = 256 sets, so the index is 8 bits. An 8-byte block needs a 3-bit offset, so the tag is 40 − 8 − 3 = 29 bits.

questions.q: A processor runs at 2 GHz. Its L1 data cache hits in 2 clock cycles, misses on 3% of accesses, and each miss adds 150 cycles to fetch the block from main memory. What is the average memory access time (AMAT) in nanoseconds?
o: 6.5 ns
76 ns
questions.kid: Grabbing a snack from the kitchen counter (the cache) takes 2 seconds. But 3 times out of 100 the counter is empty, and the trip to the garage freezer adds 150 seconds. On average a snack costs 2 + (3% of 150) = 6.5 seconds. A computer does the same math in clock ticks, then turns ticks into nanoseconds: that average is the AMAT.
questions.why: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty = 2 + 0.03 × 150 = 2 + 4.5 = 6.5 cycles. At 2 GHz one cycle is 1 ÷ (2 × 10<sup>9</sup>) s = 0.5 ns, so AMAT = 6.5 × 0.5 = 3.25 ns.
w: 6.5 is the AMAT in clock cycles; at 2 GHz each cycle is 0.5 ns, so it still has to be converted.
This counts only the 4.5 average miss cycles and drops the 2-cycle hit time that every access pays.
This charges the full 150-cycle penalty to every access, but only 3% of accesses miss.

f.q: A different design runs at 1 GHz. Its cache also hits in 2 cycles and misses on 3% of accesses, and each miss also costs 150 cycles (150 ns at this clock). What is the AMAT in nanoseconds?
f.why: AMAT is still 2 + 0.03 × 150 = 6.5 cycles. At 1 GHz a cycle is 1 ns, so AMAT = 6.5 ns.

f.q: Same 2 GHz processor and cache, but right after a cold start every access misses (miss rate 100%). What is the AMAT in nanoseconds?
Same numbers as the original: on average, how many nanoseconds per access are spent only on miss stalls, not counting the hit time?
f.why: Average miss stall = miss rate × miss penalty = 0.03 × 150 = 4.5 cycles, and 4.5 × 0.5 ns = 2.25 ns.

questions.q: A direct-mapped cache has 8 blocks and starts empty. The processor accesses the block addresses below, in order. How many of the 8 accesses are misses?
questions.kid: Picture 8 cubbies numbered 0 to 7. A toy may only go in the cubby that matches the leftover when its number is divided by 8. Toys 19 and 27 both leave 3, so they fight over cubby 3 and keep kicking each other out. Each time one comes back after the other, it has to be fetched again: a miss.
questions.why: Slot = block address mod 8: 19 → 3, 10 → 2, 14 → 6, 27 → 3. Trace: 19 M, 10 M, 14 M, 19 H, 27 M (evicts 19), 10 H, 19 M (evicts 27), 10 H. That is 5 misses: 4 compulsory (first use of 19, 10, 14 and 27) plus 1 conflict miss when 19 returns to slot 3.
w: 3 is the number of hits (8 accesses − 5 misses), not the number of misses.
4 counts only the first-time (compulsory) misses and skips the conflict miss when 19 comes back after 27 took slot 3.
6 is what you get using mod 4, as if the cache had 4 blocks; with 8 blocks, 10 and 14 go to different slots.

f.q: Same 8 blocks and sequence, but the cache is 2-way set associative (4 sets, LRU replacement). How many accesses miss?
f.why: Set = address mod 4: 19 and 27 share set 3, and 10 and 14 share set 2, but each set holds 2 blocks. Trace: M, M, M, H, M, H, H, H, so only the 4 compulsory misses remain.

f.q: Same sequence, but the direct-mapped cache has only 4 blocks (slot = block address mod 4). How many accesses miss?
f.why: Slots: 19 → 3, 10 → 2, 14 → 2, 27 → 3. Trace: M, M, M (14 evicts 10), H, M (27 evicts 19), M (10 evicts 14), M (19 evicts 27), H. That is 6 misses.

f.q: Same 8-block direct-mapped cache and the same sequence: how many of the 8 accesses are hits?
f.why: The trace M, M, M, H, M, H, M, H has 3 hits: the second use of 19 and the second and third uses of 10.

questions.q: A designer changes a 64 KiB L1 cache from direct-mapped to 4-way set associative, keeping the total capacity and the block size the same. Which outcome should she expect?
o: More conflict misses, because each block now has fewer legal places to go
Fewer conflict misses, because each block has four legal slots in its set
A shorter hit time, because only one tag has to be checked on each access
No change in miss rate, because the total capacity stays exactly the same
questions.kid: In a direct-mapped parking lot your car may only park in space #7, so if a friend's car is already there it gets towed away to make room, even when the lot is half empty, and your friend has to come back for it later. A 4-way lot gives you four spaces to pick from, so that rarely happens. The catch: the attendant has to look at four spaces to find your car, which takes a little longer.
questions.why: Higher associativity lets blocks that map to the same set live there together, which cuts conflict misses and lowers the miss rate. The cost is one tag comparator per way plus a multiplexer to choose the hitting way, so the hit time rises slightly and the hardware grows. The biggest drop in miss rate comes from 1-way to 2-way; each further doubling helps less.
w: It is the reverse: with 4 legal slots instead of 1, up to 4 blocks that share a set can stay together instead of evicting each other, so conflict misses drop.
A 4-way lookup compares 4 tags and then picks a way, which adds delay; checking one tag is the direct-mapped case.
Capacity is not the only factor: blocks that collided on one slot can now share a set, so the miss rate falls.

f.q: The designer goes the other way, from 4-way set associative to direct-mapped, at the same capacity and block size. Which benefit can she count on?
f.why: A direct-mapped cache reads one tag and compares it once, with no way-select multiplexer, so its hit time is the shortest and its hardware the simplest.

f.q: The designer goes from 4-way set associative to direct-mapped at the same capacity and block size. Which drawback should she expect?
f.why: Each block now has exactly one legal slot, so blocks that used to share a set evict each other, and conflict misses rise.

questions.q: On an ARMv8 core with 48-bit virtual addresses and 4 KiB pages, every load needs its 36-bit virtual page number mapped to a physical page number. Which hardware keeps recently used page mappings so most loads can skip reading the page table in memory?
o: The translation lookaside buffer
The page table register
The level-1 data cache
The write buffer that queues stores
questions.kid: The page table is a thick map book kept in a closet down the hall. Taped by the front door is a sticky note, the TLB, listing the handful of routes you have used today. You check the note first and walk to the closet (a page-table read) only when the route you need is missing from it.
questions.why: The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small, fast cache of page table entries. On a TLB hit the 36-bit virtual page number (48 − 12, since 4 KiB = 2<sup>12</sup>) becomes a physical page number at once, and the 12-bit page offset is copied unchanged. Only on a TLB miss does the hardware read the page table in memory, starting from the address in the page table register.
w: The page table register only holds where the current process's page table starts; it stores no translations.
The L1 data cache keeps copies of data blocks; it is the TLB that holds virtual-to-physical page mappings.
A write buffer holds stores waiting to reach memory; it plays no part in translating addresses.

f.q: Process B's page table starts at a different physical address than process A's. When the OS hands the core from A to B, which register must it reload?
f.why: The page table register holds the physical address where the running process's page table begins. Reloading it with B's table address makes every later page-table walk use B's mappings.

f.q: Which hardware keeps copies of recently used data blocks so most loads avoid a trip to main memory?
f.why: The L1 data cache holds recently used blocks of data close to the core. Keeping data is the data cache's job; the TLB keeps only translations.

f.q: With a write-through cache, which hardware lets the processor keep running while its stores wait to be written to main memory?
f.why: A write buffer queues stores so the processor does not stall for each memory write; the buffer drains to memory in the background.

questions.q: Two programs run at the same time, and each one keeps its data at virtual address 0x4000. Neither program can see or change the other's data. What makes this work?
o: The cache stores each program's blocks in a different set of slots
Each program runs on a separate core that has its own private RAM
Pages a program is not using can wait on disk until they are needed
Each program's page table maps that address to a separate physical page
questions.kid: Two kids in different houses both have a bedroom #4. A letter addressed just to "bedroom #4" needs each family's own address book to find the right house. Every program has its own address book (its page table), so the same room number leads to different real rooms, and nobody walks into the wrong one.
questions.why: Each process has its own page table, and the OS loads the page table register on every context switch. The same virtual page in two processes maps to different physical pages, and a process can reach only the pages its own table maps, so programs are protected from each other. Only the OS may change page tables.
w: Cache placement is about speed, not protection; the programs are kept apart earlier, when their addresses are translated.
Cores in one machine share the same physical memory, and the two programs would stay apart even on a single core.
Keeping idle pages on disk lets programs be larger than RAM, but it does not explain why equal virtual addresses never collide.

f.q: A 12 GiB program runs on a laptop with only 8 GiB of RAM. Which idea lets it run?
f.why: Virtual memory keeps only the pages in use in physical memory and leaves the rest on disk (swap space). A page fault brings a missing page in when it is touched, so a program can be larger than RAM.

questions.q: A program multiplies two 2,048 × 2,048 matrices of 8-byte doubles and misses in the cache constantly. The programmer rewrites the loops to work on 16 × 16 sub-matrices that fit in the cache together, finishing with each before moving on. Why does this cut the misses?
o: It lowers the number of multiply and add instructions that must run
It makes each cache hit faster, because fewer tags are checked
It reuses each piece of data many times before it can be evicted
It makes every cache block hold more of the matrix elements
questions.kid: Painting a giant mural, you could run to the paint shelf for every brushstroke all across the wall. Instead you finish one small square at a time and keep just that square's paints on your cart. Each paint gets used many times before it goes back on the shelf. That's blocking: work in tiles small enough to fit on the cart (the cache).
questions.why: Blocking (tiling) reorders the loops so a small tile of each matrix is reused many times while it is still in the cache. Three 16 × 16 tiles of 8-byte doubles take 3 × 2 KiB = 6 KiB, which fits easily in a typical 32 KiB L1 data cache, while each full matrix is 32 MiB. The arithmetic is unchanged, but capacity misses fall because data is reused before it is evicted (better temporal locality).
w: Blocking changes only the order of the work; the product still needs the same n<sup>3</sup> multiply-add steps.
Hit time is fixed by the cache hardware; reordering loops changes how often you hit, not how fast a hit is.
Block size is set by the hardware; blocking changes the order in which the loops visit data, not what a block holds.

f.q: One of the two matrices turns out to be diagonal, so the programmer skips every multiply by an off-diagonal zero. Why does the program now run faster?
f.why: Skipping the zero terms removes most of the multiply and add instructions outright. That changes how much work is done, not how well the cache is used.

questions.q: In Flynn's taxonomy, which of these machines is MIMD?
o: A 1980s home computer adding two price lists with plain ADDs, one pair at a time
A 6-core workstation running a renderer, a database and a mail server at once
A single-core image processor whose one instruction brightens 16 pixels at once
A single-core PC that switches between two open programs every 10 ms
questions.kid: Picture a kitchen with three cooks, each following a different recipe with their own ingredients: one bakes, one grills, one makes soup. Many recipes and many ingredient piles at once: that's MIMD. If one chef instead shouted "chop!" and everyone chopped their own carrot together, that would be SIMD. One cook hopping between two recipes is still just one cook.
questions.why: The workstation's 6 cores carry out independent instruction streams, each with its own data, so it is Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data. For one large job, MIMD machines are usually programmed SPMD: every core runs a copy of the same program on a different slice of the data. The single-core PC only time-slices, so it keeps one hardware instruction stream and its two programs merely take turns.
w: Its lone processor performs one ADD on one pair of prices at a time, so it is SISD, the simplest Flynn class.
One instruction acting on 16 pixels together is data-level parallelism from a single instruction stream, which makes the chip SIMD.
Switching programs every 10 ms is time-slicing: the one core still follows a single instruction stream at any moment, so nothing runs in parallel.

f.q: Same four machines: which one is SIMD?
f.why: The image processor applies one instruction to 16 pixels in lockstep (for example, 16 8-bit pixels packed into a 128-bit register), which is Single Instruction, Multiple Data.

f.q: Which of these machines handles more than one program yet carries out only one instruction stream at any moment?
f.why: The single-core PC gives each program a 10 ms turn, so the two only look simultaneous. Its hardware follows one instruction stream at a time, unlike the workstation, whose 6 cores run their streams side by side.

questions.q: A scalar loop adds two 64-element arrays one element per iteration. A vector processor does the same job with two vector loads, one vector add and one vector store. Why is the four-instruction vector version more efficient than the scalar loop?
o: Its clock ticks faster, so every cycle of the loop takes less time
Each of its element additions finishes in fewer clock cycles
It guesses the outcome of the loop branch correctly more often
It fetches far fewer instructions and checks hazards once per vector
questions.kid: A mail carrier could make 64 separate trips from the post office, one letter per house, phoning the office before each stop. Instead she gets one bundle for all 64 houses on the street and delivers it in a single run, with no calls in between. A vector instruction is that bundle: one instruction, 64 deliveries.
questions.why: Four vector instructions replace a scalar loop that executes several instructions per element, hundreds in all, so far fewer instructions are fetched and decoded. Because the 64 element additions cannot depend on each other, the hardware does one dependence check for the whole vector add, and the per-element loop branch is gone. This is data-level parallelism.
w: Vector processors do not win on clock rate; the gain comes from doing 64 operations per instruction.
Each element still goes through an adder with the usual latency; the savings come from one instruction covering all 64 additions, not from faster adds.
The vector version has no per-element loop branch at all; it removes the branch rather than predicting it better.

f.q: A scalar core replaces its fixed "predict not taken" guess with a dynamic predictor that learns the loop. Why does the same scalar loop now run faster?
f.why: The loop's backward branch is taken on every iteration but the last, so a fixed "not taken" guess is wrong almost every time. A dynamic predictor learns the pattern, guesses correctly far more often and avoids most flush penalties.

f.q: The same scalar loop runs on an identical chip clocked at 3.6 GHz instead of 3.0 GHz. Assume the CPI does not change. Why does it finish sooner?
f.why: With the same instructions and the same CPI, each cycle lasts 1 ÷ 3.6 GHz ≈ 0.28 ns instead of 1 ÷ 3.0 GHz ≈ 0.33 ns, so the run is 3.6 ÷ 3.0 = 1.2 times faster. Without that assumption the gain would be smaller, because each memory stall costs more cycles at the higher clock.

questions.q: In a two-socket server, every core can load from any address in one shared physical address space. Each core reads memory attached to its own socket in about 80 ns and memory attached to the other socket in about 130 ns. How is this machine best described?
o: A NUMA shared-memory multiprocessor
A UMA shared-memory multiprocessor
A message-passing cluster of separate nodes
A UMA multiprocessor whose second socket has slower DRAM
questions.kid: Two kitchens share one big pantry split into two rooms. Any cook can grab anything from either room, but the room beside their own kitchen is closer, so it's faster. One pantry for everybody, but different walking distances: that's NUMA, non-uniform memory access.
questions.why: All cores share one physical address space and communicate with ordinary loads and stores, so this is a shared-memory multiprocessor. Because latency depends on which core touches which memory (80 ns local, 130 ns remote), it is non-uniform memory access (NUMA). In a UMA machine every core sees the same latency to every word.
w: UMA means every core sees the same latency to every address; here it depends on which socket owns the memory.
A cluster gives each node a private address space and moves data with messages; these cores use ordinary loads to one shared space.
UMA means one latency for every core and address, and neither socket's DRAM is slow: each socket's own cores reach it in 80 ns, so the gap depends on whether the memory is local to the reading core.

f.q: A single-socket chip connects all of its cores to memory through one shared controller, so every core reads any address in about 90 ns. How is this machine best described?
f.why: One shared address space with the same latency for every core and every address is uniform memory access (UMA).

questions.q: A program spends 90% of its single-core run time on work that splits perfectly across cores; the other 10% must run on one core. By Amdahl's Law, what speedup does it get on 16 cores?
questions.kid: Friends are making sandwiches. Spreading fillings can be shared, but there's only one bread knife, and slicing is 10% of the job. Even with 16 helpers, everyone waits on that knife, so you finish only about 6.4 times faster, not 16. The part one person must do sets the limit: that's Amdahl's Law.
questions.why: Speedup = 1 ÷ [(1 − p) + p ÷ N] = 1 ÷ [0.10 + 0.90 ÷ 16] = 1 ÷ (0.10 + 0.05625) = 1 ÷ 0.15625 = 6.4. The serial 10% caps the speedup at 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 no matter how many cores are added. This is strong scaling: the problem size stays fixed.
w: 16× would need 100% of the work to be parallel; the serial 10% still takes as long as before.
10× is the ceiling with unlimited cores (1 ÷ 0.10); 16 cores cannot reach it.
14.5 = 0.1 + 0.9 × 16 is the scaled speedup when the problem grows with the cores (weak scaling), not this fixed-size run.

f.q: Same program (10% serial), but now with an unlimited number of cores. What is the largest speedup Amdahl's Law allows?
f.why: As N grows, 0.90 ÷ N approaches 0, so the speedup approaches 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10.

f.q: Instead of a fixed problem, the parallel work grows 16 times along with the 16 cores (weak scaling) while the serial part stays the same. What is the scaled speedup?
f.why: On 16 cores the run still takes 0.1 + 0.9 = 1.0 time unit. One core would need 0.1 + 0.9 × 16 = 14.5 units for the bigger problem, so the speedup is 14.5.

f.q: Same 16 cores, but the program has no serial part at all: 100% of it splits perfectly. What is the speedup?
f.why: With p = 1, speedup = 1 ÷ (0 + 1 ÷ 16) = 16.

questions.q: A team runs a fluid simulation on 8, then 64, then 512 nodes. Each time they enlarge the grid so every node always handles about 2 million cells, and the run time stays nearly flat. Which term describes this experiment?
o: Weak scaling of the simulation
Strong scaling of the simulation
Load imbalance among the nodes
Amdahl's Law limit on speedup
questions.kid: If one kid can paint one fence in an hour, then 8 kids can paint 8 fences in an hour, and 512 kids can paint 512 fences in an hour. The job got bigger as more kids joined, and the time stayed the same. That's weak scaling. Strong scaling would be 512 kids squeezing onto one fence.
questions.why: Weak scaling grows the problem in proportion to the processor count so the work per processor stays constant: 2 million cells per node means 16 million cells on 8 nodes and about 1 billion on 512. A flat run time means it scales well. Strong scaling keeps the total problem fixed and is limited by Amdahl's Law, because the serial part never shrinks.
w: Strong scaling keeps the total problem fixed as nodes are added; here the grid grows from 16 million to about 1 billion cells.
Load imbalance means some nodes get more work than others while the rest sit idle; here every node gets the same 2 million cells.
The Amdahl's Law limit is the cap a serial part puts on the speedup of a fixed-size problem; growing the problem with the nodes is how weak scaling escapes it.

f.q: The team instead keeps the grid at 64 million cells and runs it on 8, 64 and 512 nodes to see how much sooner it finishes. Which term describes this?
f.why: A fixed total problem spread over more and more processors is strong scaling, and its speedup is bounded by Amdahl's Law.

questions.q: A server core runs two hardware threads with coarse-grained multithreading. Which event makes it set the running thread aside and start the other one?
o: The start of each new clock cycle, whatever the running thread is doing
A cycle in which one thread leaves some of the issue slots empty
A 1-cycle bubble while an ADD waits on the load just ahead of it
A load that must wait about 300 cycles for its data to come from DRAM
questions.kid: A cashier helps one customer until that customer has to run back to the car for a wallet, a long wait, and then serves the next person in line. If a customer only pauses a second to sign, the cashier just waits, because switching would take longer than the pause. Switching only on the long waits is coarse-grained multithreading.
questions.why: A thread switch empties the pipeline, and the other thread must refill it before its instructions complete, which costs several cycles. A coarse-grained core therefore switches only for a wait long enough to repay that cost, such as a 300-cycle trip to DRAM, and simply sits through a 1-cycle bubble. Fine-grained multithreading instead rotates threads every cycle, and SMT mixes instructions from both threads within one cycle.
w: Rotating threads on every clock tick describes fine-grained multithreading; this core keeps the same thread running until something slow happens.
Filling one thread's empty issue slots with the other thread's instructions in the same cycle is SMT; a coarse-grained core issues from only one thread at a time.
A 1-cycle bubble is over long before a switch could empty and refill the pipeline, so the core just waits it out.

f.q: The same two-thread core is rebuilt to use fine-grained multithreading. When does it now move from one thread to the other?
f.why: A fine-grained core interleaves its threads cycle by cycle, issuing from the other ready thread every clock, so it switches at each new cycle whether or not anything has stalled.

f.q: A 4-wide out-of-order core runs its two threads with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) instead. When do the second thread's instructions issue alongside the first thread's?
f.why: SMT lets both threads compete for the 4 issue slots every cycle, so whenever one thread cannot fill all 4, ready instructions from the other thread take the empty slots in that same cycle.

f.q: Under coarse-grained multithreading, which of these stalls is too short to be worth a thread switch?
f.why: Emptying the pipeline and refilling it with the other thread costs several cycles, more than the bubble itself, so the core stays on the same thread and lets the bubble pass.

questions.q: Each trip from a GPU to its graphics memory takes hundreds of clock cycles, yet the GPU's arithmetic units stay busy. How does it hide that memory latency?
o: It keeps the whole working set in a very large last-level cache
It switches among many hardware threads, running whichever are ready
It predicts branches and runs one thread's instructions far out of order
It issues several instructions per clock from each thread (superscalar)
questions.kid: A pizza shop with dozens of orders never lets its cooks stand around. While one pizza bakes (waiting), the cook starts the next order, then the next. With enough orders going, there is always something ready to work on. That's how a GPU hides waiting: tons of threads, and it switches to whichever is ready.
questions.why: GPUs rely on hardware multithreading, not large multilevel caches, to hide memory latency. Each multithreaded SIMD processor keeps many groups of threads resident; when one group waits on memory, the scheduler issues from another that is ready. GPU memory is built for bandwidth rather than low latency, and many threads in flight keep it and the arithmetic units busy.
w: GPU caches are small compared with the data they stream, so GPUs do not count on caches to cover memory latency.
Deep speculation and out-of-order execution are CPU techniques; GPU cores issue each thread's instructions in order.
Wider issue only speeds up instructions that are ready; a thread waiting hundreds of cycles on memory soon has nothing it can issue.

f.q: A server CPU runs one thread whose 40 MiB of data fits entirely in the chip's 64 MiB last-level cache, so it almost never waits on DRAM. How does it avoid memory latency?
f.why: With the whole working set held on chip, nearly every access hits in the large last-level cache. That is the usual CPU strategy: a deep cache hierarchy instead of many threads.

f.q: A single-threaded desktop CPU keeps working past a slow load by executing later independent instructions and guessing which way branches go. How does it hide latency?
f.why: Out-of-order execution with branch prediction and speculation finds independent work inside one thread, which is how CPUs hide latency without extra threads.

questions.q: A lab links 32 rack servers through an Ethernet switch and runs one large job on all of them, each server running a copy of the same program. Which statements describe this cluster? (Select all that apply.)
o: Each node has its own private memory and runs its own copy of the OS
Any core can read another node's memory with an ordinary load instruction
Nodes share data by explicitly sending and receiving messages
Since every node runs the same program, the cluster counts as SIMD
questions.kid: Think of pen pals in different towns. Each one has their own house and stuff, and nobody can reach into anybody else's drawer. To share anything, they mail a letter. A cluster works the same way: each computer keeps its own memory and sends messages to share data.
questions.why: A cluster is a set of whole computers, each with its own memory and OS, joined by a network. With no shared address space, one node cannot load another node's data, so programs move data with explicit send and receive calls (for example MPI). Running the same program on every node is SPMD, a way to program MIMD hardware, not SIMD.
w: Cluster nodes have separate address spaces; one node cannot load from another's memory, so data must travel as a message.
One program on many independent processors is SPMD on MIMD hardware; SIMD means one instruction applied to many data items in lockstep.

f.q: In a NUMA shared-memory server built from several nodes (sockets), how can a core use data that sits in another node's memory?
f.why: A shared-memory multiprocessor has one physical address space, so a core simply issues an ordinary load; the hardware fetches the data from the remote node, just more slowly.

questions.q: A perfectly parallel job takes 120 seconds on one core. It is split across 4 cores, but one core is given 40% of the work and the other three get 20% each. Ignoring overhead, what speedup over one core does it get?
questions.kid: Four kids clean a house. One gets the kitchen (a big job) and the other three get small closets. The closet kids finish fast and then sit and wait. The house isn't clean until the kitchen kid is done, so the busiest helper sets the finish time, which is why sharing the work evenly (load balancing) matters.
questions.why: Parallel time is set by the busiest core: 0.40 × 120 s = 48 s, while the others finish at 0.20 × 120 s = 24 s and sit idle. Speedup = 120 ÷ 48 = 2.5, compared with 120 ÷ 30 = 4 for a perfect 25% split. Balancing the load matters as much as adding cores.
w: 4× needs each core to get exactly 25% of the work; with 40% on one core, the others finish early and wait.
3.0× divides 120 by 40, reading the 40% share as 40 seconds; 40% of 120 s is 48 s, and that busiest core sets the finish time.
This treats the 40% share as serial work done before the rest starts; in fact all four cores run at the same time.

f.q: Same 120-second job on 4 cores, but now each core gets exactly 25% of the work. What is the speedup?
f.why: Each core runs 0.25 × 120 = 30 s, so the speedup is 120 ÷ 30 = 4.

f.q: Same 120-second job on 4 cores, but now one core gets a third of the work and the other three share the rest equally. What is the speedup?
f.why: The busiest core runs 120 ÷ 3 = 40 s, while the other three run 80 ÷ 3 ≈ 26.7 s each, so the speedup is 120 ÷ 40 = 3.0.

f.q: Same 4 cores, but the 40% share must finish on one core before the other 60% can start, split evenly across the remaining 3 cores. What is the speedup?

questions.q: A loop adds two arrays of 4,096 16-bit integers. It uses ARM SIMD instructions on 128-bit registers with H (16-bit) lanes, and each vector ADD works on one full register. How many vector ADD instructions does the loop need?
questions.kid: A 128-bit register is like a tray 128 inches wide. Each 16-bit number takes 16 inches, so 8 fit on a tray. One SIMD add handles a whole tray at once, so 4,096 numbers need 4,096 ÷ 8 = 512 trays.
questions.why: A 128-bit register split into H (16-bit) lanes holds 128 ÷ 16 = 8 elements, so one vector ADD performs 8 additions. 4,096 elements ÷ 8 per instruction = 512 vector ADDs. The ARM lane suffixes are B = 8-bit, H = 16-bit, S = 32-bit and D = 64-bit; Q names the whole 128-bit register.
w: 1,024 assumes 4 lanes per register, which is S (32-bit) lanes; 16-bit H lanes fit 8 per register.
256 assumes 16 lanes per register, which is B (8-bit) lanes; 16-bit elements fill only 8 lanes.
4,096 is one add per element, the scalar count; each SIMD ADD here does 8 additions at once.

f.q: Same loop and 128-bit registers, but the arrays hold 32-bit integers in S lanes. How many vector ADD instructions are needed?
f.why: 128 ÷ 32 = 4 lanes, so 4,096 ÷ 4 = 1,024 vector ADDs.

f.q: Same loop and 128-bit registers, but the arrays hold 8-bit integers in B lanes. How many vector ADD instructions are needed?
f.why: 128 ÷ 8 = 16 lanes, so 4,096 ÷ 16 = 256 vector ADDs.

f.q: The same 4,096 additions of 16-bit integers are done with ordinary scalar ADD instructions, one element each. How many ADDs are needed?
f.why: A scalar ADD handles one element, so 4,096 elements need 4,096 ADDs, 8 times as many as the SIMD version.

questions.q: A hypervisor runs two guest operating systems on one server, and each guest kernel runs at a lower privilege level than the hypervisor. Guest A's kernel executes a privileged instruction that turns off interrupts. On a processor built to support virtualization, what happens?
o: It runs directly and turns off interrupts on the real core
It silently does nothing, and guest A carries on as if it worked
The hypervisor shuts guest A down, because guests may never use privileged instructions
Only guest A's virtual interrupts are turned off; the hypervisor keeps the real ones
questions.kid: Two families rent rooms in one house, and the landlord (the hypervisor) keeps the keys to the main fuse box. If one family tries to flip the main breaker, the landlord steps in and switches off only that family's lights. The other family never notices a thing.
questions.why: On a virtualizable processor, every privileged instruction traps when it runs below the top privilege level. The hypervisor (VMM), running at the highest level, catches the trap and emulates the instruction on guest A's virtual state, marking only guest A's virtual interrupts as disabled while the real interrupt system stays under its control. Hardware support such as Intel VT-x or ARMv8's EL2 can keep this per-guest state in hardware without a trap. Either way guest A behaves as if it owned the hardware, and guest B stays isolated.
w: Letting a guest change real machine state would break isolation; only the hypervisor may control the real interrupt system.
Quietly ignoring the instruction is the flaw of ISAs that are not fully virtualizable; guest A would then misbehave.
Guests may issue privileged instructions; the hypervisor emulates their effect for that guest instead of shutting it down.

f.q: The same OS runs alone on bare metal in the most privileged mode, with no hypervisor. What happens when its kernel executes this instruction?
f.why: With no hypervisor, the OS is the most privileged software, so the instruction executes directly and turns off interrupts on the real core that runs it.

f.q: On an older ISA, the instruction that turns off interrupts is not privileged: at low privilege it neither traps nor changes the interrupt setting. What happens when guest A executes it?
f.why: Nothing traps, so the hypervisor never sees the instruction; the interrupt setting is left alone while guest A wrongly believes interrupts are off. The x86 POPF instruction behaved this way, which made classic x86 hard to virtualize.

questions.q: A guest OS runs under a hypervisor. The guest's page table maps virtual page 0x2A to frame 0x113. What is frame 0x113?
o: A guest "real" frame, which the hypervisor maps again to a host physical frame
A physical frame that the hardware can use with no further mapping
A frame owned by another guest, which the two guests share
A guest virtual page, which the guest OS translates a second time
questions.kid: A tour leader hands out her own room list: "You're in room 3." But the hotel front desk keeps a second list that turns her room 3 into the actual hotel room 512. Getting to your bed takes two lists: the leader's (the guest OS) and the front desk's (the hypervisor).
questions.why: Under a hypervisor there are three levels: guest virtual, guest "real" and host physical memory. The guest OS's page tables map virtual pages to real frames, and the hypervisor's tables map real frames to physical frames. To avoid paying for both lookups on every access, the hypervisor can keep a shadow page table that maps guest virtual pages straight to host physical frames.
w: That holds only without a hypervisor; a guest's frame numbers are one mapping away from the hardware.
Each guest's real frames belong to that guest; the hypervisor keeps guests isolated unless it deliberately maps a shared page.
A page table outputs frame numbers, not virtual pages; the guest OS translates each virtual page once, and only the hypervisor adds a second mapping.

f.q: The same OS runs directly on the hardware with no hypervisor. What is frame 0x113 in its page table?
f.why: Without virtualization there is only one mapping: the OS's page table maps virtual pages straight to physical frames, so 0x113 is a physical frame the hardware uses directly.

f.q: To skip the second lookup, the hypervisor builds a shadow page table for this guest. What does the shadow entry for virtual page 0x2A hold?
f.why: A shadow page table combines the guest's map and the hypervisor's map, so each entry maps a guest virtual page directly to a host physical frame the hardware can use.

questions.q: A hypervisor stops running VM 2 on a core so that VM 3 can run there. Which items must it save so that VM 2 can later resume exactly where it left off? (Select all that apply.)
o: Its registers, including the program counter
A copy of every memory page it owns
Its page table register
The contents of the caches it was using
questions.kid: Two cooks share one stove. When cook A steps away, she clips a card to the rail with the recipe step she is on (the program counter), what is in each of her bowls (the registers) and which shelf holds her ingredients (the page table register). Her ingredients stay on her shelf, so nothing else has to move.
questions.why: A VM's (or process's) state is its registers, its program counter and its page table. Its memory pages stay where they are, kept apart from other VMs by the page tables, so the hypervisor saves VM 2's registers, PC and page table register (the pointer to its page table), then loads VM 3's values. Caches need no saving: they are managed by hardware and tagged by physical address, so VM 2's blocks stay correct (dirty ones are written back when evicted) and VM 3's accesses simply miss and refill.
w: The pages stay in memory, protected by the page tables; copying all of them on every switch would be far too slow and is not needed.
Caches are managed by hardware: VM 2's blocks stay correct, dirty ones are written back when evicted, and VM 3's misses simply refill them, so they are not part of the saved state.

f.q: The hypervisor live-migrates VM 2 to a different physical server. Besides VM 2's registers and page table pointer, which listed item must it also send?
f.why: The new server has its own separate memory, so VM 2's memory pages must be copied over before it can resume there.

f.q: Right after the switch, VM 3 runs slowly for a moment because of a burst of misses. Which listed item still holds mostly VM 2's data and so causes those misses?
f.why: The caches are not saved or reloaded on a switch, so right after it they still hold mostly VM 2's blocks. VM 3's first accesses miss and refill the caches from memory, which is why it starts slowly.

questions.q: A three-person startup has written its own web app. Traffic jumps tenfold every weekend, so the team wants capacity that grows and shrinks automatically and bills only for what is used. They also do not want to install or patch operating systems. Which choice fits best?
o: IaaS: rent virtual machines by the hour
PaaS: deploy code to a managed platform
SaaS: subscribe to a ready-made application
On-premises: buy and run your own servers
questions.kid: Think of a caterer who rents a fully equipped commercial kitchen by the hour. The caterer just brings the recipes; the owner keeps the ovens and plumbing working and opens more stations on busy weekends. That's PaaS: you bring the code, and the provider runs everything underneath it.
questions.why: Cloud service models differ in who manages what. IaaS rents virtual machines, but the customer installs and patches the OS and everything above it; PaaS runs the customer's code on an OS and runtime that the provider manages and scales automatically; SaaS delivers a finished application. Like other cloud offerings, PaaS is elastic and pay-per-use, so the weekend spike costs extra only while it lasts.
w: IaaS can also scale and bill by use, but the team would still install and patch the OS on every virtual machine.
SaaS is a finished product run by someone else; the startup needs to run its own app.
Owned servers must be bought for the weekend peak, sit mostly idle on weekdays and still need patching, the opposite of elastic pay-per-use.

f.q: The team now needs to choose its own operating system and change kernel settings, but still wants to rent capacity by the hour. Which choice fits best?
f.why: IaaS gives the customer virtual machines with full control of the OS, while the provider still owns the hardware and bills per use.

f.q: A different company has no app of its own; it just needs email and shared documents for its staff. Which choice fits best?
f.why: SaaS delivers ready-made applications, such as email or office suites, that the provider runs and maintains.

f.q: A contract requires the company to own its hardware and keep it in its own locked server room. Which choice fits best?
f.why: Owning the servers and housing them in the company's own room means running on premises; the IaaS, PaaS and SaaS offerings listed here are rented and run on a provider's hardware.

questions.q: A file server's six 10 TB drives are set up as RAID 6. How much usable space does it have, and how many drive failures can it survive at once?
o: 50 TB; survives any one failure
60 TB; survives no failures
30 TB; survives one failure per mirrored pair
40 TB; survives any two failures
questions.kid: Imagine spreading one cookbook across six binders, splitting the recipes among them. Then you add check notes (parity) worth two binders' pages, spread across all six. That leaves four binders' worth of pages for recipes, and the notes can rebuild any two binders that go missing.
questions.why: RAID 6 keeps two independent parity blocks in every stripe, spread across all the drives, so it gives up two drives' worth of space and survives any two failures at once: (6 − 2) × 10 TB = 40 TB usable. RAID 5 keeps one parity block per stripe, (6 − 1) × 10 TB = 50 TB, and survives one failure; RAID 0 keeps all 6 × 10 TB = 60 TB with no redundancy; three mirrored pairs keep 6 × 10 TB ÷ 2 = 30 TB and survive one failure in each pair.
w: 50 TB and one failure describe RAID 5, which keeps only one parity block per stripe; RAID 6 keeps two.
60 TB and no protection describe RAID 0 striping; RAID 6 gives up two drives' worth of space to parity.
30 TB and one failure per pair describe mirroring; RAID 6 protects data with parity, not mirrored pairs.

f.q: The same six 10 TB drives are set up as RAID 5 instead. How much usable space is there, and how many drive failures can it survive at once?
f.why: RAID 5 spreads one parity block per stripe across the drives: (6 − 1) × 10 TB = 50 TB usable, and it survives any single failure.

f.q: The same six 10 TB drives are striped as RAID 0 instead. How much usable space is there, and how many drive failures can it survive?
f.why: RAID 0 stripes data across all six drives with no redundancy: 6 × 10 TB = 60 TB usable, and losing any one drive loses data.

f.q: The same six 10 TB drives are set up as three mirrored pairs instead. How much usable space is there, and how many drive failures can it survive?
f.why: Each pair stores the same data twice, so half the raw space is usable: 6 × 10 TB ÷ 2 = 30 TB. The data survives as long as every pair keeps one working drive, so it can lose one drive in each pair, but not both drives of the same pair.

questions.q: A warehouse-scale computer has 73,000 servers, and each server has a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 20 years (175,200 hours). Assuming failures are spread evenly over time, about how often will a server fail somewhere in the building?
o: About once every 20 years
About 0.4 times per day
About 10 times per day
About 200 times per day
questions.kid: One light bulb that lasts 20 years almost never needs changing. But a stadium with 73,000 of those bulbs sees about ten burn out every day, just because there are so many. A huge data center is the same: with enough servers, something is always breaking.
questions.why: Failures per day ≈ number of servers ÷ MTTF in days = 73,000 ÷ (20 × 365) = 73,000 ÷ 7,300 = 10. Each server rarely fails, but at warehouse scale failures are routine, so the software and the facility must be designed to tolerate them through redundancy.
w: Once every 20 years is the rate for a single server; 73,000 servers fail 73,000 times as often.
About 0.4 is the rate per hour (73,000 ÷ 175,200 ≈ 0.42); per day it is 24 times larger.
200 per day would need an MTTF of just 1 year (73,000 ÷ 365), not 20 years.

f.q: Same 73,000 servers, but each has an MTTF of only 1 year. About how often will a server fail?
f.why: 73,000 ÷ 365 days = 200 failures per day.

f.q: A small cluster has 2,920 servers with the same 20-year MTTF. About how often will one fail?
f.why: 2,920 ÷ 7,300 days = 0.4 failures per day, or about one every two and a half days.

f.q: Only one such server is running. About how often will it fail?
f.why: A single server with a 20-year MTTF fails, on average, once every 20 years.
